lines.direction: Flat. Does not look up from whatever he is eating.

lines.text: No.
I've been in that room. It has a very strong opinion about itself.
Mine has a water stain shaped like Ohio.
Cars don't wear trench coats.
It's not your birthday.
It was on a bridge. It was a hard parade to find.
The container number's on the news. P-A-C, four-four-seven-one.
The pretzel guy is the same guy who runs the wheel.
I'd prefer we spoke elsewhere. I don't care for being overheard.
Ash. Detective Rowan, Port Alder police. I hope this isn't a bad time. I think we might be interested in the same shipment.
lines.direction: Calm, courteous. A man who has never needed to raise his voice.

lines.text: There's a bench in City Plaza by the clock tower. Public place. Nobody will be taking notes. I'd like to buy you a coffee and trade a few facts.
lines.direction: A short pause. He lets it sit.

lines.text: Now, Ash. What do I tell my captain? What did you find at the warehouse?
lines.direction: Gently, as if the tape had not played. He has made himself a person with nothing to hide.

lines.text: Thank you. That is exactly what I needed to know. I'll see it is handled properly.
lines.direction: A very small smile. He has what he came for.

lines.text: Of course. We'll keep this between us.
lines.direction: Studying Ash for exactly one second too long. Then pleasant.

lines.text: A wise caution. I will remember that you offered it.
lines.direction: Very calm. The temperature in the yard drops a degree.

lines.text: The holding yard, north of the station. I will meet you at the gate. Stay in your car until I wave you in. The officers on duty are good people. They don't need to remember you.
lines.direction: On the phone, driving ahead. Even, unhurried.

lines.text: Thank you for coming. Sit. The coffee is better than it has any right to be.
lines.direction: Seated, two coffees on the bench. Pleasant, measured. He doesn't stand.

lines.text: I did. Let me start with mine. For eighteen months this department has been trying to understand a pattern. Stolen vehicles. Cargo that goes missing from the port and comes back as something else. Evictions in places that are conveniently quiet at night.
lines.direction: A thin smile. He is not offended.

lines.text: Every time we get close, someone higher up reminds us that the port is a political subject. I won't name them. You would learn nothing.
I'm a cautious one. That's often the same thing from a distance.
lines.direction: A very small pause. His eyes do not move.

lines.text: The warehouse. I understand you went through rack nine, behind the blue containers. I understand someone was waiting at the gate with a flashlight. And I understand you did not take what you came for.
The incident report.
Reports are very thorough, when I'm the one who writes them.
lines.direction: He sips his coffee. A deliberate silence. Then he says it as if it were nothing.

lines.text: I have access to an evidence room that has seen better days. If you'll let me, I'd like to show you something you may find useful. And in return, I'd like to know what you took.
And I suspect you've already decided what to do with whatever you found. I only ask that you hear me out.
lines.direction: Mild. He has read the room.

lines.text: Let's be precise. They'll find only what I put in front of them.
lines.direction: Recorded, distorted, a man who does not want to be heard. Flat. Precise.

lines.text: The cameras are on a loop. I wouldn't take the loop personally.
lines.direction: Quiet, a hand on the gate. He glances once at the cameras.

lines.text: I can do a number of things.
Box four, on the right. Property from a locker at Berth Nine, taken five years ago. Nobody ever signed for it.
lines.direction: Pointing, without pointing, at a stack of boxes under a tarpaulin.

lines.text: I could tell you that was a missing person case that was never closed. It isn't my case to open. It is, apparently, yours.
lines.direction: Gentle, with the patience of a man who has told this story before.

lines.text: Evidence. I haven't listened to it. I'd prefer someone with less to lose did.
lines.direction: The first real silence. Then, smoothly.

lines.text: Ash. Good evening. You're in a restricted area. I'd advise you step away from the container.
lines.direction: Calm, courteous, almost sorry. A police radio murmurs behind him.

lines.text: I'm always quick. It's the only reason I've lasted.
There are four patrol cars at the gate. They will not harm you if you put the cabinet down. I'd much rather this were quiet.
Ash. I think we should speak before anyone else arrives.
lines.direction: Arriving alone, coat buttoned. The same calm voice. It no longer sounds like control; it sounds like fatigue.

lines.text: Let's be precise. I was, and I am not proud of it.
lines.direction: A very long pause. Longer than any pause he has used.

lines.text: I joined to make a difference. In the first years, I did. Then someone made a call about my daughter's tuition, and the next day a report was misplaced, and the day after that I was the person who misplaced them. It is remarkably easy. That's what I would like you to understand. It is not a decision; it is a series of small mercies you grant yourself.
lines.direction: Slowly. He is speaking to someone who is not Ash.

lines.text: Now I have a cabinet of evidence to arrest and a conscience that has become, inconveniently, very loud.
lines.direction: Dry. Almost a smile. His hands are open at his sides.

lines.text: Officer Whitfield. I was very much hoping it would be you.
lines.direction: Studying her. Then, very quietly, a faint, relieved, broken exhale.

lines.text: I do. How very precise of you.
lines.direction: A pause. Then something that is almost a laugh.

lines.text: No. But it would have been nice to borrow one.
Port Alder is changing. Alder Point: a waterfront for everyone. Jobs, homes, and a skyline we can all be proud of. Sloane Development. Building what comes next.
lines.direction: Calm, polished radio-ad voice. Warm, never salesy.

lines.text: Mr. Ash. Or Ms. Ash. I'm told the preference doesn't matter. Victor Sloane. Thank you for coming to the reception.
lines.direction: Smooth, courteous, arriving as though the room were his. He holds out a hand and takes his time.

lines.text: Ms. Cruz. A pleasure. Your family has been delivering to the waterfront for years. We value that, as I'm told they value us.
I understand you've been touring Wharf Street. It's a disgrace what has happened there, honestly. I'm trying to help those people leave before it gets worse. It's the only decent thing to do.
lines.direction: To Ash, the soft focus of a man doing a favour.

lines.text: Emotional people say remarkable things. You and I are practical, I think. May I be practical?
lines.direction: A gentle, rueful smile. He is not threatened. He is delighted to be understood.

lines.text: I have a project that will employ four thousand people. A handful of unhappy owners are a regrettable cost. I'd like to prevent anyone from being hurt.
lines.direction: Steady, as if reading out a menu.

lines.text: Twenty thousand dollars. In return, a quiet understanding: that whatever you've borrowed, you will return, and whatever you're planning to say, you will say nothing at all. It isn't a threat. It is, if anything, a very generous kind of advice.
lines.direction: Taking out an envelope and leaving it on the table between them, very gently.

lines.text: Take a moment. I have all evening.
lines.direction: Mild. He has heard her and ignored it with perfect manners.

lines.text: That is all anyone can ask. Thank you. I'm sure we will understand each other.
lines.direction: Delighted, and not showing it too much.

lines.text: Very well. I regret that. I do hope the two of you stay safe in the city. It can be unpredictable.
lines.direction: Not a flicker of anger. He picks it up, and puts it away like a man putting away a pen.

lines.text: A practical answer. I do appreciate practical people.
Enjoy the evening. The shrimp are excellent. Please don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
lines.direction: Parting, courteous. He is already looking at someone else in the room.

lines.text: Port Alder is changing. Alder Point: a waterfront for everyone. Now open to the public. Sloane Development. Building what comes next.
lines.direction: The radio ad again, ever so slightly changed. Gentle, wry, satisfied.

lines.text: Ash. Good evening. I wondered whether you would find your way here.
lines.direction: In the lobby of Harbor Tower at night, alone, immaculate, holding a cufflink. He greets Ash as if they had agreed to meet.

lines.text: I am always alone. It's what keeps one from getting sentimental.

You have a cabinet of paper. I have a city. If you give it to a reporter, a number of people will lose their jobs, and some will lose more than that. The project will fail. Four thousand jobs. The waterfront will be left as it was, derelict, until it is eventually bought by someone less patient.
lines.direction: Calm. As if describing a weather system.

lines.text: You accepted my envelope once. I did notice. It tells me a great deal about you. I think we could do business.
You refused my first offer. I admired it. I hope you will forgive me for making a better one.
Fifty thousand dollars. A clean record. A new life. A place at the table, if you want one. Or an end to it all, if you prefer. There is room for you in whatever I build next.
lines.direction: Taking a slim folder from his jacket. He makes it sound like a gift.

lines.text: The alternative is that you give it away, and a great many people will be very angry with you, including some I can no longer restrain.
Including this.
lines.direction: Tilting his head. He is, for the first time, mildly interested.

lines.text: How very impractical of you.
lines.direction: A small, almost admiring exhale. The first unplanned sound he has made.

lines.text: That's all I ever wanted. A practical conversation.
That is, I think, rather foolish.
lines.direction: For the first time, a flicker of alarm.

lines.text: Alder Point. A waterfront for everyone. Sloane Development. Building what comes next.
It's been sitting there. I never could look at it. Tell Eddie it still runs.
lines.direction: Handing over the keys without being asked. Quiet.

lines.text: Somebody had to. Danny would've kept it for me.
Don't talk to me around the cameras.
lines.direction: Sitting on a bollard. Gruff, not looking at Ash.

lines.text: The tide comes in and goes out. People think it's the sea. It's the moon. Nobody ever thanks the moon.
You're not Tony.
lines.direction: Gruff, suspicious, a man who has been burned by new faces.

lines.text: Hm.
lines.direction: Walking slowly around the pickup, looking at the tailgate.

lines.text: Who had it before Eddie got it? Before the paint.
lines.direction: Careful. Pretending it's a casual question and failing.

lines.text: There was a dent here. Shaped like a boot. Big man kicked it, one night, over a gate that wouldn't open. You see a boot dent?
lines.direction: Crouching, thumb on the tailgate where something should be.

lines.text: Huh. Somebody fixed a lot of things on this truck.
lines.direction: Quiet. He stands, and he does not like what he is thinking.

lines.text: Tell Eddie thanks. Don't tell him I asked about the dent. It ain't my business.
lines.direction: Signs the paper without reading it. Low, like he regrets saying anything.

lines.text: You again. The truck kid.
lines.direction: Tired, at the fence, a flashlight in his hand. He recognises the driver from the pickup.

lines.text: That case ain't here.
lines.direction: A long exhale. The name is a weight he already carries.

lines.text: He said a lot of things. Everything on that rack was cleared this afternoon. Forklift, flatbed, gone. Nobody told me. Nobody told the paper either.
lines.direction: Low. He glances at the camera on the pole and keeps his voice under it.

lines.text: That ain't my business.
lines.direction: Flat. He has said it before, to himself.

lines.text: Rack nine. Back of the building, behind the blue containers. They left a few. If you're going to look, don't take long. Alarm wasn't armed this morning and it's been armed since lunch.
lines.direction: A long look. Something moves behind his face and goes back.

lines.text: I thought I'd be braver.
lines.direction: Sitting on the lighthouse step, one hand pressed to his ribs. Out of breath. Alive.

lines.text: In a lighthouse. Hiding. Very brave.
I'm not going anywhere!
I said I was fishing.
lines.direction: In the shadow of the door, a thermos in his hand. He doesn't come out. He sounds ten years older than at the docks.

lines.text: No. I don't.
Because the boy who made that dent was Danny Vale. And the last time I saw him, he gave me an envelope and said, "If I don't come in Tuesday, give it to somebody who isn't scared."
lines.direction: Long silence. Then, haltingly, as if he has been practising the first line for five years.

lines.text: He didn't come in Tuesday. I wasn't that person. I've been waiting five years to find out who was.

A copy of the Berth Four gate log. The night PAC-4471 left without a signature. Four names on it. One of them is a detective. One of them is a man who doesn't do his own lifting. And one of them I recognise from the radio ads.
lines.direction: Taking a worn envelope from inside his coat. His hands are shaking.

lines.text: I saw Danny's truck go out that night with two men I'd never seen before. It came back two days later. Danny never did.
lines.direction: He nods, once. It's the nod of a man handing something heavy to someone younger.

lines.text: I know I should've said something. I just kept thinking, ain't my business. It's been everybody's business the whole time.
lines.direction: Quiet. He looks at Ash for the first time.

lines.text: They're here.
lines.direction: Headlights sweep the road below. His voice drops to nothing.
